markers.name: ApoB
markers.description: Apolipoprotein B — count of atherogenic particles. The single best lipid predictor of cardiovascular risk.
markers.guidance: Responds to saturated-fat intake, soluble fibre, weight, and — strongly — to statins or ezetimibe when lifestyle alone isn't enough. Track it after any diet change; it moves within 6–12 weeks.
markers.label: BORDERLINE HIGH

markers.name: LDL-C
markers.guidance: Moves with the same levers as ApoB, but particle count (ApoB) is the better conversation to have with your doctor — LDL-C can look fine while particle count stays high.
markers.label: BORDERLINE HIGH

markers.name: HDL-C
markers.guidance: Raised by aerobic exercise, weight loss, and quitting smoking. Very high values aren't extra protection; the optimal band is enough.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Triglycerides
markers.description: Blood triglycerides — a marker of metabolic health.
markers.guidance: The fastest lipid to move: refined carbs and alcohol push it up, exercise and omega-3s pull it down. A true fasting draw matters here.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Lp(a)
markers.description: Lipoprotein(a) — largely genetic, independent cardiovascular risk factor.
markers.guidance: Mostly genetic — lifestyle barely moves it. Worth knowing once; if elevated, it sharpens how aggressively the other lipid targets should be treated.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: HbA1c
markers.guidance: A 3-month average, so it responds slowly — judge changes over quarters, not weeks. Moves with weight, muscle mass, sleep, and post-meal walks.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Fasting glucose
markers.guidance: Sensitive to the previous day's sleep, stress, and late meals. One odd reading means little; the trend across draws is the signal.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Fasting insulin
markers.description: Fasting insulin — early marker of insulin resistance.
markers.guidance: The earliest metabolic warning light — rises years before glucose does. Strength training and reduced refined-carb load are the main levers.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: hs-CRP
markers.guidance: Reflects systemic inflammation; spikes with illness, hard training, and injury — never draw it while sick. Persistent elevation is the pattern worth discussing.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Ferritin
markers.description: Iron stores. Low ferritin drives fatigue even before anemia.
markers.guidance: Low ferritin drives fatigue long before anemia shows. Responds to supplementation over ~3 months; pair iron with vitamin C and recheck rather than over-supplementing.
markers.label: BORDERLINE LOW

markers.name: Iron saturation
markers.guidance: Read alongside ferritin — together they separate true iron deficiency from inflammation or overload.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Hemoglobin
markers.guidance: Falls with iron deficiency or blood loss; a key endurance and energy marker. Slow-moving, so trend it across draws.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Testosterone, total
markers.guidance: Supported by strength training, quality sleep, and healthy body composition; suppressed by chronic stress, poor sleep, and excess body fat.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Vitamin D (25-OH)
markers.guidance: Most people need sun plus supplementation to reach the optimal band, especially in Canadian winters. Recheck after 8–12 weeks on a new dose.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: TSH
markers.guidance: The first thing that shifts when thyroid output drifts. A single borderline value is worth repeating before acting on it.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: ALT
markers.guidance: Elevated by fatty liver, alcohol, and some medications; improves with weight loss and less alcohol. Mild elevations are common and worth trending.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Creatinine
markers.guidance: Influenced by muscle mass and hydration, so athletes often run higher — it's read together with eGFR, not alone.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: eGFR
markers.guidance: Higher is better; a stable trend matters far more than any single reading. Dips can reflect dehydration as much as kidney function.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: WHOOP Recovery
markers.guidance: Blends HRV, resting heart rate, and sleep into one readiness score — a guide for how hard to train today, not a diagnosis.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: HRV
markers.guidance: Higher signals a well-recovered nervous system. Driven by sleep, training load, alcohol, and stress; compare to your own baseline, not to others.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Resting HR
markers.guidance: A rising multi-day trend often flags fatigue, illness, or overtraining before you feel it. Very individual — watch the direction.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Sleep
markers.guidance: The single biggest lever on recovery, HRV, and next-day performance. Consistency of timing matters as much as total hours.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Weight
markers.description: Body weight. No universal target — the trend against your own goal is the signal, not the level.
markers.guidance: Judge the 7-day average, never a single morning — water swings 1–2 kg day to day. Same scale, same time, same conditions makes the trend trustworthy.
markers.label: TRACKED

markers.name: Blood pressure (systolic)
markers.description: The top number — arterial pressure while the heart beats. Home and pharmacy cuff readings are worth logging; a single reading means little, the pattern means a lot.
markers.guidance: Responds to sodium, alcohol, sleep, aerobic exercise, and stress. Measure seated, rested, arm supported — and log a few readings across different days before drawing conclusions.
markers.label: OPTIMAL

markers.name: Blood pressure (diastolic)
markers.description: The bottom number — arterial pressure between beats. Log it alongside systolic; the pair reads together.
markers.guidance: Moves with the same levers as systolic. If home readings run high across a week, that pattern — not any single number — is what to bring to your doctor.
markers.label: OPTIMAL
